response:
KV cache eviction policy design asks: given a fixed GPU memory budget, which cached key-value tensors do you discard when a new sequence needs space, and how does that choice ripple back into prefill latency? The central tension is that eviction isn't free — evicting a sequence that later gets requeued forces a full prefill recomputation, turning what looked like a memory win into a latency spike. Heterogeneous sequence length distributions sharpen this problem because short and long sequences have wildly different cache footprints and reuse probabilities; a policy tuned for a narrow length distribution (say, chat-style 200-token turns) will thrash badly when suddenly hit with 8k-token document queries that each consume 40x the cache space of a short request. The key concepts are: cache hit rate as a function of eviction order, prefill latency as a deterministic cost paid on every cache miss, and the variance (not just mean) of that latency — because high variance is what breaks SLO tail latency guarantees even when average latency looks fine. What a beginner misses is that eviction policy interacts with the scheduler: if your eviction policy quietly discards sequences that the scheduler intended to resume, you get a hidden feedback loop where the scheduler's queuing assumptions become invalid, causing bursts of simultaneous cache misses and correlated prefill storms rather than the smooth load the scheduler modeled.

LRU evicts the least-recently-used sequence regardless of its memory footprint, which works acceptably when sequence lengths are roughly symmetric — but under right-skewed distributions (the common real-world case where most requests are short and a fat tail is long), LRU systematically over-retains many small sequences while being forced to evict them in bulk the moment one large sequence arrives, because a single 8k-token sequence can consume the same cache space as 40 short 200-token sequences. The cost of that bulk eviction isn't symmetric either: each evicted short sequence costs one prefill recomputation of ~200 tokens, but the probability it gets requeued quickly is high (short sessions tend to have rapid back-and-forth), so you pay the recomputation cost frequently. A size-aware policy like ORCA's length-aware scheduling or the approach described in the RadixAttention work (SGLang, Zheng et al. 2024) reframes the eviction unit from "sequence" to "tokens of KV cache," allowing it to preferentially evict large low-reuse sequences first and preserve the dense cluster of short high-reuse ones. The concrete benefit is cache hit rate stability: under heavy skew, RadixAttention-style prefix reuse reported hit rates above 80% for shared-prefix workloads where pure LRU would drop below 40% once long sequences start competing for space. What the size-aware policy trades away is implementation complexity and the need to estimate reuse probability at eviction time — if your reuse signal is wrong (e.g., you assume long sequences are low-reuse but a document QA workload repeatedly queries the same long context), size-aware eviction degrades worse than LRU because it evicts exactly the sequences that were actually hot. The skewness therefore doesn't just shift the average-case performance gap between policies; it amplifies the sensitivity to reuse estimation error, making the choice of eviction policy tightly coupled to workload characterization.

The strongest observable signal is inter-arrival time (IAT) of requests sharing the same prefix or session ID — if a session has shown sub-second IAT historically, its cached KV state is almost certain to be reused within the next few seconds, whereas sessions with IAT above the median eviction window are effectively cold. vLLM's prefix caching implementation implicitly exploits this by keying cache blocks on prefix hashes, which means hit rate is directly observable per prefix and can seed a lightweight frequency counter without any model inference. The second-best signal is request position within a multi-turn session: first-turn requests have unknown reuse probability, but any request with turn index ≥ 2 has already demonstrated continued engagement, and the conditional probability of a third turn given a second is empirically high (Chatbot Arena logs suggest multi-turn sessions have 3-5 turns on average, so turn 2 still has substantial continuation probability). Sequence length itself is a weak but nonzero signal: very long sequences (say, >4k tokens) in a chat workload are disproportionately one-shot document processing tasks with near-zero reuse, while mid-length sequences (500–2k tokens) in the same workload tend to be active reasoning sessions. Client-side metadata, where available — API key tier, endpoint type, or whether the request carries a system prompt identical to a cached one — is underexploited; production systems like Anthropic's and OpenAI's that serve both batch and interactive endpoints could use endpoint type as a near-perfect reuse discriminator, since batch jobs virtually never reuse KV state across calls. The practical danger is that these signals are all correlated with each other and with time-of-day load patterns, so naively combining them without regularization will overfit to a particular traffic mix and fail silently when the workload shifts.

The core architectural answer is to decouple scoring from the allocation hot path entirely: maintain a priority queue of eviction candidates that is updated asynchronously by a background thread, so that the allocator during prefill only needs to pop the queue head rather than compute a score — this is essentially what PagedAttention in vLLM does for its block allocator, where the free-block list is maintained separately from inference execution. The scoring function must therefore be incrementally maintainable: rather than recomputing a score from scratch on every access, you update a small set of counters (last-access timestamp, hit count, owning session's IAT estimate) in O(1) on each request arrival, and the eviction score is a cheap arithmetic combination of those counters readable in a few nanoseconds. The danger of even cheap per-block scoring is that at high request rates (say, 1000 req/s with 16 blocks per sequence), you're touching the scoring metadata for ~16k blocks per second, which creates false sharing on the cache metadata array if blocks belonging to different sessions are laid out contiguously in memory — NVIDIA's FasterTransformer and later vLLM both learned this and aligned block metadata to cache lines to avoid the coherence traffic. A practical bound from production systems: block allocation decisions need to complete in under ~10 microseconds to stay off the critical path of a typical prefill that itself takes milliseconds, which means your eviction scorer has a budget of roughly 1-2 microseconds per decision, easily met by a linear combination of 3-4 integer counters but not by anything involving a hash lookup or branch-heavy logic per block. The subtler issue is that scoring granularity should be at the sequence or prefix level, not the individual block level — blocks within a sequence are never partially evictable in current systems (you can't evict layer 12's KV for a sequence while keeping layer 11's), so per-block scores are wasted precision; scoring per logical sequence and then evicting all its blocks atomically reduces metadata overhead by a factor equal to average sequence length in blocks, typically 8-64x.

The fundamental constraint is that you cannot evict blocks belonging to a sequence that is currently resident in a running batch — the GPU kernels executing that decode step hold implicit references to those physical block addresses, and evicting them would corrupt live attention computation with no recoverable error signal. vLLM resolves this with a two-color reference counting scheme: blocks have a "logical" reference count incremented when a sequence is scheduled into a batch and decremented only after the decode step completes and outputs are written back, so the eviction candidate pool is strictly the set of blocks with zero logical references — preemption candidates are sequences waiting in the queue, not sequences currently decoding. The atomicity requirement therefore pushes eviction pressure onto queued sequences rather than running ones, which creates an asymmetry: under memory pressure, the scheduler must either preempt a queued sequence (cheap, no GPU state to save) or, if all memory is held by running sequences, stall new prefills entirely until a decode step completes and releases blocks — this stall is the mechanism behind the latency spikes observed in vLLM under heavy load documented in the Sarathi-Serve paper (Agrawal et al. 2023), where prefill stalls of 50-200ms appeared when the KV cache filled during large batch decode. Copy-on-write adds another layer: when a sequence is forked for parallel sampling, vLLM marks shared blocks as copy-on-write rather than duplicating them, and eviction must treat the entire shared subtree as a unit with reference count equal to the number of live forks — evicting one fork's blocks without decrementing shared-block references correctly will leak memory silently. The practical implication for scheduler design is that the eviction policy and the batch composition policy must share a single consistent view of block reference counts, updated under a lock or via a lock-free atomic protocol, because a race between the scheduler promoting a queued sequence to running and the evictor selecting that sequence's blocks as candidates will produce a use-after-free on the GPU — this is why Sarathi and later systems like MoonCake serialize eviction decisions inside the same scheduling loop iteration rather than running them concurrently.

The optimization target is minimizing P99 prefill latency rather than mean, which changes the answer significantly: a policy that maximizes average cache hit rate will over-invest in the prefix cache reservoir, leaving insufficient headroom for burst absorption, because a single burst that exhausts running-batch headroom causes a cascade of prefill stalls that dominates the tail. The theoretically clean framing is to model the system as two competing queues sharing a memory budget — running batch blocks are a hard reservation (non-evictable), prefix cache blocks are a soft reservation (evictable under pressure) — and set the partition point where the marginal latency cost of shrinking the prefix cache by one block equals the marginal latency cost of shrinking the running batch headroom by one block; in practice this means the prefix cache should be sized to absorb expected inter-burst idle time reuse, not peak load reuse. Empirically, MoonCake (Qian et al. 2024) found that on their production cluster, reserving roughly 20-30% of KV cache capacity as non-evictable running-batch headroom and treating the remaining 70-80% as evictable prefix cache achieved near-optimal P99 latency, compared to the naive 100% evictable allocation which saw P99 spikes 3-5x higher during bursts because headroom exhaustion triggered simultaneous preemptions. The bursty arrival pattern specifically punishes static partitions because burst intensity is heavy-tailed — a partition tuned for median burst size will be overwhelmed by the 95th-percentile burst, so the better approach is a dynamic watermark: when free evictable blocks drop below a threshold (say 15% of total), the scheduler begins throttling new prefills to let decode steps drain and release blocks before admitting more sequences. The subtle second-order effect is that prefix cache hit rate is itself burst-dependent: during a burst, many requests share prefixes and hit rate is high, meaning the cache earns its memory more during bursts than during idle periods — this argues for a dynamic partition that expands the prefix reservoir during high-hit-rate periods and contracts it (releasing headroom) when hit rate drops, which is the adaptive approach taken in InfiniGen and hinted at in the Preble scheduling system.

The interaction mechanism is a priority inversion: SLO-aware admission control ranks requests by deadline or tier and admits the highest-priority ones first, but a watermark throttle is SLO-blind — it blocks all new prefills regardless of their deadline, meaning a high-priority request with a tight SLO can sit behind the watermark barrier while lower-priority requests already in the running batch continue decoding, directly inverting the intended service order. The watermark set too high (too conservative, triggers early) causes unnecessary prefill starvation: decode steps keep running but no new prefills enter, so GPU utilization drops and the queue of waiting requests grows faster than the watermark clears, creating a self-reinforcing stall that Sarathi-Serve documented as "prefill bubbles" — in their measurements, an overly conservative watermark reduced throughput by 15-20% while paradoxically increasing P99 latency because queued requests aged past their SLO deadlines waiting for a watermark that didn't need to be held that long. The watermark set too low (too aggressive, triggers late) fails its original purpose: memory exhaustion occurs before throttling engages, forcing emergency preemptions of queued sequences, each of which costs a full prefill recomputation on requeue — this is strictly worse than proactive throttling because it adds recomputation latency on top of the queueing latency. The correct interaction is to make the watermark SLO-aware by maintaining separate admission queues per SLO tier and applying the watermark only to best-effort traffic, allowing latency-sensitive requests to bypass the throttle up to a secondary hard memory limit — this is architecturally what Orca's iteration-level scheduling and later Llumnix's migration-based scheduling approximate, though neither fully solves the priority inversion cleanly. The deeper problem is that the watermark threshold is not a single correct value but a function of current decode batch size, per-step token generation rate, and arrival rate — all of which are nonstationary, meaning a static watermark will be miscalibrated during workload shifts, and the correct engineering answer is a control-theoretic feedback loop (proportional to queue growth rate) rather than a fixed threshold, an approach prototyped in the Shepherd serving system but not yet standard in production inference engines.

The minimum state set for a provable P99 bound is four quantities sampled at each scheduling iteration: current running batch size in tokens (not sequences, because token count determines GPU step time), current free evictable block count, empirical per-step decode latency as an exponential moving average, and the arrival rate estimate over a short window (roughly 1-5 seconds) — from these four you can compute a first-order estimate of time-to-memory-exhaustion and compare it against the P99 latency budget to decide whether to throttle. The provability claim requires one additional assumption: that decode step latency is bounded above by a known constant for a given batch token count, which holds under static batching but becomes stochastic under continuous batching with variable output lengths — this is why systems like Sarathi-Serve chunk prefills into fixed-size pieces, because chunking makes per-step latency deterministic and therefore makes the controller's time-to-exhaustion estimate tight rather than a loose upper bound. The instrumentation overhead of tracking these four quantities is genuinely low: batch size and free block count are maintained by the allocator already at zero marginal cost, per-step latency requires one clock read per scheduling iteration (nanoseconds), and arrival rate requires a token-bucket counter update on each request admission — the total overhead is under 1 microsecond per scheduling iteration, which is negligible against the millisecond-scale scheduling loop. The reintroduced latency risk is more subtle than raw overhead: the moving average window for arrival rate creates a phase lag, meaning the controller responds to the arrival rate that existed 1-5 seconds ago rather than the instantaneous rate, and during a sharp burst onset that lag allows memory pressure to build before throttling engages — the window length is a direct tradeoff between noise rejection and burst responsiveness, and there is no universally correct value. The honest answer about provable bounds is that they require stationary arrival statistics, which real workloads violate — the Shepherd and Llumnix papers both acknowledge that their controllers provide empirical P99 improvements (30-50% reduction in tail latency in their evaluations) rather than hard guarantees, because the non-stationarity of LLM serving workloads makes formal queueing-theoretic bounds loose to the point of uselessness in practice.
